title: Show HN: Mnemolith – AI coding memory that goes stale when your code changes

item.text:
Hi HN, I'm Anish. I built Mnemolith because the AI coding tools I use (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) either forget my project between sessions, or remember things that quietly stopped being true. Tell the agent "we use Postgres", migrate to MySQL two weeks later, and it keeps building on the old fact.

How it works:

- It's an MCP server, so Claude Code, Cursor and Codex share one memory per project (keyed by the git repo). - When the agent saves a memory, it can link it to the files it depends on. Mnemolith stores each file's git blob hash. If the file's contents change (committed or not), the memory is set aside and flagged for review, so the agent stops relying on it. - A local dashboard shows what the agent remembers, where each memory came from (tool, session, file versions), and its full history. You can confirm a memory is still true, or retire it and say what's true now. - Contradictions are judged by the agent, not by a similarity threshold. In my calibration, "we use Postgres" vs "we migrated to MySQL" only scored 0.30 similarity, so a threshold can't tell a contradiction from an unrelated fact. - Current memories can sync into a managed section of AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, so they get reviewed in PRs.

Under the hood it runs on an engine I wrote from scratch in Java: a Redis-compatible server with a built-in memory model and an HNSW vector index. Embeddings run locally (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Everything stays on your machine.

It's early (v0.2.1). There's no team sync yet beyond the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files, and it needs Java 11+ (it downloads a private copy if you don't have one).

I'd really like feedback, especially from people running coding agents on real codebases. What does your agent keep getting wrong?
item.title: Show HN: Mnemolith – AI coding memory that goes stale when your code changes

sources.text:
Mnemolith
Shared memory for AI coding tools that stays true to your code.
Mnemolith (NEE-mo-lith): "memory stone." What your AI learns, carved where every tool can read it. (
Why the name
)
Formerly Aether Cache.
If you installed
aether-cache
, see
Moving from Aether Cache
: your memories come with you.
Website
·
PyPI
Claude Code, Cursor, and other AI tools each forget your project between sessions, and when they do remember things,
nothing checks whether those memories are still correct. Mnemolith gives every tool one shared, local memory, and keeps
it honest:
Memories go stale when the code changes.
Each memory is linked to the files it's about, with a snapshot of their
git content hash. When
docker-compose.yml
changes, the memory about it is retired automatically instead of being
fed to your AI forever.
Contradictions get replaced, not hoarded.
"We migrated to MySQL" retires "we use Postgres" instead of sitting
next to it and confusing the model. Near-identical repeats are merged.
Every memory can explain itself.
Which tool and session saved it, which file versions it was based on, and every
change since: created, seen again, went stale, confirmed, replaced.
It works with the files you already use.
Current memories sync into a managed section of
AGENTS.md
and
CLAUDE.md
, so they're committed, reviewed in PRs, and visible to teammates who don't run Mnemolith.
It runs entirely on your machine, on top of a database engine I wrote from scratch.
Not a Redis clone
Mnemolith started as a from-scratch rebuild of Redis in Java, then kept going. Every layer here is written from
scratch, and each one does something the layer beneath it can't:
Layer
What it adds
MCP server
Claude Code, Cursor, and any MCP tool share one memory
Git awareness
Memories retire themselves when the code they describe changes
Memory layer
Status, provenance, full history, duplicate merging, and conflict review, inside the engine
HNSW vector index
Semantic search: 99.4% recall at 0.84 ms on 100K vectors, 22× faster than exact search
Redis-compatible engine
RESP protocol, 50+ commands, replication, transactions, and crash-safe persistence (0 acknowledged writes lost across 1,039,890 writes and 8
kill -9
crashes), at 88–93% of real Redis's throughput
The bottom layer alone is a working Redis:
redis-cli
,
redis-benchmark
, and
redis-py
talk to it unchanged. The
memory layer, git awareness, and MCP server are things Redis doesn't do at all.
Claude Code ─┐                       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
Cursor ──────┼─ MCP ─► mnemolith ─┼─ RESP ─► Java engine (Main.java)            │
other tools ─┘   (Python: embeddings,│          memories, HNSW vector index,       │
git hashing, sync) │          history, append-only file on disk  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
What it looks like
The dashboard (
mnemolith ui
): memories whose files changed wait for a decision, with the file versions side by side.
And from your AI tool's side, a memory linked to a file, the file changes, and the next lookup catches it:
> remember("The database runs Postgres via docker compose", files=["docker-compose.yml"])
Saved as m1.
... someone edits docker-compose.yml ...
> recall("database setup")
These memories were just retired because files they depend on changed. If one is still true,
call confirm_memory; if it's wrong, save the corrected fact with remember:
[m1] "The database runs Postgres via docker compose" is now marked outdated: docker-compose.yml changed.
> confirm_memory("m1")        # still true, so re-link it to the new version of the file
Confirmed m1; it's active again and linked to the current file versions.
> explain_memory("m1")
m1: "The database runs Postgres via docker compose"
status: active, project: demo
saved by: claude-code (session eea54b5c)
linked files: docker-compose.yml@02ea346...
history:
19:16  created: by claude-code (session eea54b5c), linked to docker-compose.yml@87da641...
19:16  active -> stale: docker-compose.yml changed since this was saved
19:16  re-linked: to docker-compose.yml@02ea346... (confirmed still true)
19:16  stale -> active: confirmed still true
A newer fact replacing an older one:
> remember("The API timeout was raised to 60 seconds")
Saved as m3.
Related existing memories:
[m1] (similarity 0.58) The API timeout is 30 seconds
If m3 makes any of these no longer true, call replace_memory(old_id, "m3"). Otherwise do nothing.
> replace_memory("m1", "m3")
m1 retired; m3 replaces it.
Quick start
One line installs everything and runs setup. On macOS or Linux:
curl -fsSL https://mnemolith.dev/install.sh
|
sh
On Windows (PowerShell):
powershell
-
ExecutionPolicy ByPass
-
c
"
irm https://mnemolith.dev/install.ps1 | iex
"
The installer (
install.sh
,
install.ps1
) gets
uv
if you
don't have it (uv brings Python), installs Mnemolith, and runs
mnemolith setup
. Prefer your own tools? Any of
these works, followed by
mnemolith setup
:
uv tool install mnemolith
pipx install mnemolith
pip install mnemolith
#
Python 3.10+
setup
starts the engine in the background, downloads the embedding model once (about 90 MB), and connects every
supported AI tool it finds on your machine:
Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex
. That's it. Open your AI tool in any git
repo and try:
Remember that our tests need DOCKER_HOST set. It depends on docker-compose.yml.
Then start a new session and ask how to run the tests.
The engine runs on Java 11+. If you have it, it's used. If you don't, Mnemolith downloads a private copy (about
50 MB) into
~/.mnemolith/java
, checks it against its published checksum, and uses it only for Mnemolith;
nothing is installed system-wide, and
mnemolith uninstall
removes it.
Already keep notes for your AI in
CLAUDE.md
,
AGENTS.md
, or Cursor rules? Run
mnemolith import
in the repo
(or use
Import notes
in the dashboard) to turn them into memories, linked to the files they mention.
Memories are kept per project (the git repo's folder name), so projects never mix. Everything stays on your machine:
the engine only accepts connections from it, and your memories live in
~/.mnemolith
.
Command
What it does
mnemolith setup
One-time setup: engine, model, and AI tools
mnemolith add
Adds the repo you're in (or a path) so the dashboard can check its files; the dashboard can also find and add repos for you
mnemolith ui
Opens the dashboard: see what your AI remembers, and confirm or retire memories whose files changed
mnemolith import
Turns the notes in
CLAUDE.md
,
AGENTS.md
, and Cursor rules into memories; shows them first and asks
mnemolith export
Saves memories, with their linked files and history, to a JSON file (
-p
for one project)
mnemolith status
Is it running, and what's in this project's memory
mnemolith doctor
Checks everything and tells you how to fix what's wrong
mnemolith list
/
recall "query"
/
explain m1
Look at memories from the terminal
mnemolith sync
Writes current memories into
AGENTS.md
/
CLAUDE.md
mnemolith connect cursor
Connects one tool (
--print
shows config for any other MCP tool)
mnemolith start
/
stop
Runs or stops the engine (it also starts on its own when a tool needs it)
mnemolith uninstall
Disconnects your AI tools, stops the engine, and asks before deleting memories
If
mnemolith
isn't found after installing, run
uv tool update-shell
and open a new terminal. Port 7380 taken?
Set
MNEMOLITH_PORT
and run
setup
again. To uninstall:
mnemolith uninstall
, then
uv tool uninstall mnemolith
.
Moving from Aether Cache
Mnemolith used to be called Aether Cache. If you installed
aether-cache
, run the installer above. It installs
Mnemolith, removes
aether-cache
, moves your memories from
~/.aether-cache
to
~/.mnemolith
, and reconnects your AI
tools. Nothing is lost, and memories synced into
CLAUDE.md
/
AGENTS.md
are picked up where they are.
Installed some other way? Install
mnemolith
the same way, run
mnemolith setup
, then remove
aether-cache
(
uv tool uninstall aether-cache
,
pipx uninstall aether-cache
, or
pip uninstall aether-cache
).
Tools the AI can call
Tool
What it does
remember(fact, files?)
Saves a durable fact, optionally linked to files. Merges near-identical repeats and shows related memories so the AI can decide whether the new fact replaces one.
recall(query, limit?)
Searches the project's memories by meaning. Checks linked files first, so it never returns a memory whose code changed underneath it.
explain_memory(id)
Where a memory came from and its full history.
replace_memory(old, new)
Retires an older memory that a newer one makes untrue.
mark_outdated(id, reason)
Retires a memory that turned out to be wrong.
confirm_memory(id)
Brings back a memory that's still true after its files changed, re-linked to the current versions.
check_stale()
Runs the file check on demand.
list_conflicts()
/
resolve_conflict(...)
Reviews pairs of very similar memories that may contradict each other.
sync_to_files()
Writes current memories into
AGENTS.md
/
CLAUDE.md
(also:
mnemolith sync
).
Design decisions, and what the measurements said
Similarity can't detect contradictions, so the AI judges
The first version flagged a new memory as a possible contradiction when it was similar to an existing one. Calibrating
with real
all-MiniLM-L6-v2
embeddings showed that can't work:
Pair
Kind
Similarity
"we use Postgres" / "the database is Postgres"
duplicate
0.73
"tests need DOCKER_HOST set" / "you have to set DOCKER_HOST before running tests"
duplicate
0.92
"we use Postgres" / "we migrated to MySQL"
contradiction
0.30
"API timeout is 30 seconds" / "API timeout is 60 seconds"
contradiction
0.94
"tests need DOCKER_HOST set" / "integration tests need a running Redis"
related, both true
0.34
Duplicates scored 0.73 to 0.92 and contradictions 0.30 to 0.94, so no threshold separates them. A threshold low enough
to merge real duplicates would silently merge "timeout is 30s" with "timeout is 60s", the worst bug this product could
have. So the engine only auto-merges near-identical text (similarity ≥ 0.97). For everything else, embeddings
find
the related memories and the AI, which already understands the sentences,
decides
whether one replaces another.
Staleness compares file contents, not commits
Each linked file is stored as
path@<git blob hash>
, computed with
git hash-object
. Comparing contents rather than
commit ids catches uncommitted edits, ignores commits that didn't touch the file, and needs no git hooks:
recall
re-hashes the handful of linked files before every search.
Memories never mutate silently
Every change is a logged event with a timestamp and a reason. The engine logs each memory
with
the id and timestamp
it assigned, so replaying the log after a restart rebuilds the exact same memories and histories, down to the
millisecond, instead of minting new ones.
The engine underneath
A Redis-compatible server written from scratch in Java. It speaks RESP, so
redis-cli
,
redis-benchmark
, and
redis-py
work with it unchanged. The core was built by completing every stage and extension of the
CodeCrafters "Build Your Own Redis"
challenge; the vector index,
persistence hardening, and the memory layer are my own additions.

JVM GC / JIT pauses
Typical latency is on par with Redis. The gap is in worst-case latency, from JVM garbage collection and JIT warm-up,
which Redis (written in C) doesn't have.
HNSW vector search vs. exact search

all-MiniLM-L6-v2
(384 dimensions, cosine similarity), 500 held-out queries,
k = 10. Recall is measured against exact brute-force search on the same data.

At ef=100, HNSW returns 99.4% of the true top-10 about
22× faster
than exact search. Building the index for 100K
vectors took 136 seconds (M=16, M0=32, efConstruction=200). Latencies are measured from the Python client, so they
include network and client overhead. Full setup and raw numbers:
results.json
.
How it works:
each vector links to its nearest neighbors in a layered graph. A search starts on a sparse top layer
of long-range links, hops greedily toward the query, drops down a layer at a time, and finishes with a best-first search
on the bottom layer that keeps the
ef
best candidates. Neighbor selection uses the diversity heuristic from the HNSW
paper (prefer neighbors in different directions over near-duplicates), which is what keeps recall high.
Filtered search:
HNSW doesn't know about memory status, so searches over-fetch candidates, drop the ones that don't
match (stale or superseded), widen the search if too few survive, and fall back to an exact scan if needed. In a test
with 2,000 memories where only 2% were active, filtered searches returned exactly the correct top 10 on 30/30 queries.
The catch: at that selectivity, the exact fallback runs most of the time, which is the known weak spot of
post-filtering on graph indexes.
Crash safety
Every write goes to an append-only file (AOF) that is replayed on startup.
kill -9
crash test
(
crash_test.py
): a client writes as fast as it can, the server is killed at a random moment,
restarted, and every write the server acknowledged is checked.
fsync policy
Crashes
Acknowledged writes
Lost
everysec
5
757,295
0
always

282,595
0
Recovery took 0.6 seconds per restart, replaying up to ~185K writes.
Torn writes:
a machine crash can cut the last write off halfway. The first version refused to start on such a file;
now replay stops at the last complete command, trims the partial one, and starts normally with all earlier data intact.
Cost of each fsync policy
(SET throughput, 50 clients):
Policy
Throughput
p50 latency
always
(sync every write)
42.9K/sec

(sync once a second)
113.9K/sec

no
(let the OS decide)
118.8K/sec
0.103 ms
everysec
is 2.7× faster than
always
and within 4% of
no
, which is why it's the sensible default. On macOS,
fsync
doesn't force the SSD's own cache to flush, so
always
looks cheaper here than it would on a Linux server.

Running the engine on its own
java src/main/java/Main.java
#
port 6379
java src/main/java/Main.java --bind 127.0.0.1
#
accept connections from this machine only
java src/main/java/Main.java --port 6380 --replicaof
"
localhost 6379
"

Reproducing the benchmarks
Each benchmark runs against the engine you've started:
redis-benchmark -p 6379 -t set,get
#
throughput; also run against redis-server to compare
python vector_bench.py
#
HNSW recall and latency (start the engine with -Xmx4g)
python crash_test.py everysec 5
#
kill -9 crash test
python memory_mcp/calibrate.py
#
embedding similarity calibration
Related work
Mnemolith is an early, open-source project. These are the production systems in the same space:
Vector search in Redis-style stores:
Redis 8 vector sets
and
valkey-search
add HNSW vector search to Redis and Valkey.
hnswlib
is the reference HNSW implementation.
Malkov & Yashunin (2016)
is the paper this index follows.
Memory for AI agents:
Mem0
,
Zep
,
Letta
, and the
MCP reference memory server
.
Instruction files:
AGENTS.md
and
CLAUDE.md
. Mnemolith syncs into these rather than
replacing them.
Status and limitations
Mnemolith is v1 and early. It works end to end in automated tests and is now being tried in real Claude Code sessions.
Not done yet:
A with-memory vs. without-memory evaluation
on real coding tasks, to measure whether it actually reduces
re-explaining.
AOF compaction:
the log only grows, and every status change adds a line.
Engine limitations:
Threading:
one OS thread per connection, not an event loop. That's fine for a local tool, but it won't scale to
thousands of clients like Redis.
Transactions:
EXEC
isn't isolated, so other clients' commands can interleave with a transaction's commands.
Vector index:
re-adding a vector updates it without rewiring its graph links, and there's no delete. Retired
memories are filtered out, not removed.
Replication:
full resync only, and a new replica assumes the master's dataset is empty.
Smaller gaps:
KEYS *
lists only string keys.
GEOSEARCH
scans every member.
ACL supports only the
default
user.
HELLO
(RESP3) isn't supported, so clients must use RESP2.
Project layout
src/main/java/Main.java      the engine (single file, from the CodeCrafters setup)
mnemolith/                   the Python package behind the `mnemolith` command
server.py                  MCP server: embeddings, git staleness, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md sync
engine.py                  finds Java, starts and stops the engine in the background
javart.py                  downloads a private copy of Java when the computer has none
connect.py                 registers Mnemolith with Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex
cli.py                     the `mnemolith` command
ui.py, ui/index.html       the dashboard (`mnemolith ui`): a local server, its API, and the page
portability.py             import from notes files, export to JSON
engine/mnemolith-engine.jar the prebuilt engine (rebuild with `python scripts/build_engine.py`)
memory_mcp/calibrate.py      similarity calibration for duplicate/contradiction thresholds
vector_bench.py              HNSW benchmark (writes results.json)
crash_test.py                kill -9 crash-safety test

release workflow
